newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: U.N. agencies pull staff out of Tajikistan.
newsitem.headline: U.N. agencies pull staff out of Tajikistan.

text.p: The United Nations on Friday said it was withdrawing all non-essential personnel from Tajikistan after a spate of kidnappings.

"In view of the serious security situation in Dushanbe and danger to the lives of United Nations personnel, United Nations special representative Gerd Merrem...has decided to relocate UNMOT (military observers) and all other U.N. agencies from Tajikistan to Uzbekistan," said a statement given to journalists in the Tajik capital Dushanbe.
Only essential personnel would remain, it said.

The Red Cross announced on Thursday it was suspending operations in the former Soviet state after two employees, Elizabeth Trinch of Britain and her Tajik translator, were abducated. They were released on Friday and returned to the capital Dushanbe.

But four employees with the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR), including a Nigerian, four U.N. military observers from Austria, Switzerland and Ukraine -- and four Russian reporters kidnapped earlier this week were still held by rebels.
The hostage-takers are part of a group commanded by Rizvon Sadirov, who used to fight for the Islamic opposition forces but whose loyalties are now unclear.
The kidnappings were carried out by Rizvon's brother Bakhrom Sadirov, who is demanding free passage for other members based in neighbouring Afghanistan to return to Tajikistan.
Earlier, the Tajik government said the remaining hostages could be released on Friday.
"The negotiations are hopeful," Zafar Saidov, spokesman for Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov, said. "The others are expected to be released tonight," he said.
But a helicopter sent tentatively to collect the remaining hostages returned empty on Friday evening.

"The helicopter returned from Obigarm empty," Capt Artur Gulko, spokesman for the mainly Russian peacekeeping force in Tajikistan which sent the helicopter, told Reuters. He did not say why the hostages had not been released.

Tajikistan, a mountainous country bordering China, has been racked by a four-year civil war but a ceasefire between the government and the armed Islamic opposition last December appears to be holding.
